overview.text: Merfolk—mermaids and mermen—are fictional folklore beings usually imagined with a human upper body and a fish tail. Traditions give them varied appearances, origins, and personalities, so they are not one fixed character type. They matter as figures people have used to imagine the mysterious sea, appearing in stories and European map art as wondrous or threatening beings. They are distinct from Homer’s Greek Sirens: Homer does not describe their appearance, and Greek art showed them with human heads and bird bodies; later representations shifted until they resembled mermaids. A reported mermaid sighting by Columbus in 1492 is understood as a manatee encounter, not evidence of merfolk.

key_facts.text: The Smithsonian describes mermaid traditions as varied in appearance, origin, and personality.
The Smithsonian identifies Oannes, a Babylonian god, as the earliest recorded half-human, half-fish figure in its account.
Homer’s Odyssey does not describe the Sirens’ looks; Greek art depicted them with human heads and bird bodies, while later portrayals made them resemble mermaids.
The Smithsonian reports Columbus’s 1492 mermaid sighting as an encounter with a manatee, rather than a real mermaid.
A 1550 map by Pierre Desceliers depicts a siren admiring herself among ships, showing how such sea beings appeared in map art.
